title: Personal finance basics
subtitle: Core ideas explained, general education not advice

cards.prompt: What is it called when you earn interest not only on your deposit but also on interest already earned?
cards.example: Compound interest turns small, steady savings into surprisingly large sums over decades.
cards.note: Each year's interest is added to the balance and earns interest itself, so growth speeds up over time. The longer the time span, the stronger the effect.

cards.prompt: You deposit 100 at 10% interest per year, compounded yearly. What is the balance after two years?
cards.example: After two years the account shows 121, not 120, because the second year also paid interest on the first year's 10.
cards.note: Year one: 100 x 1.10 = 110. Year two: 110 x 1.10 = 121. The extra 1 is interest on interest, the seed of compounding.

cards.prompt: What is the general rise in prices over time called?
cards.example: Inflation means the same basket of groceries costs more this year than it did last year.
cards.note: When prices rise, each unit of money buys a little less. Many central banks aim for low, stable inflation of around 2% per year.

cards.prompt: Your savings earn 2% per year while inflation is 3%. What happens to your purchasing power?
cards.example: It falls in real terms, even though the balance on the statement keeps growing.
cards.note: What counts is the real return: interest minus inflation. Here that is about 2% minus 3%, so roughly minus 1% per year.

cards.prompt: Using the rule of 72, roughly how long does money take to double at 6% per year?
cards.example: At 6% a year, 72 divided by 6 gives about 12 years to double.
cards.note: Divide 72 by the yearly percentage to estimate the doubling time. It works both ways: at 3% inflation, prices double in about 24 years.

cards.prompt: What is spreading money across many different investments to reduce risk called?
cards.example: Diversification means one company going bust barely dents a portfolio that holds hundreds.
cards.note: The idea is 'don't put all your eggs in one basket'. It lowers the risk of a single failure, but it cannot remove the risk of the whole market falling.

cards.prompt: What is a common guideline for the size of an emergency fund?
cards.example: A common guideline is to keep 3 to 6 months of expenses in an easily accessible account.
cards.note: This buffer covers surprises like a broken car or a job loss without forcing you into debt. It is a rule of thumb: people with less stable income often aim for the upper end.

cards.prompt: What is a fund called that simply tries to track a market index?
cards.example: Index fund investors do not try to beat the market, they try to copy it.
cards.note: Index funds are passively managed, which usually keeps their costs low. Their return closely follows the index minus fees.

cards.prompt: What does ETF stand for?
cards.example: Exchange-traded fund shares can be bought and sold on a stock exchange throughout the trading day.
cards.note: An ETF is a fund whose shares trade on an exchange like a stock. Many ETFs track an index, but not all of them do.

cards.prompt: What is the yearly cost of a fund, shown as a percentage of the money invested, called?
cards.example: Expense ratio figures look small, yet 0.2% still means about 2 per year for every 1,000 invested.
cards.note: It is taken out of the fund automatically, so you never see a bill. In Europe the same figure is usually called TER, total expense ratio.

cards.prompt: At 6% yearly growth over 30 years, about how much smaller is the end result if fees take 1% more per year?
cards.example: About a quarter less money is left after 30 years of growing at 5% instead of 6%.
cards.note: 1.06 to the power of 30 is about 5.74, while 1.05 to the power of 30 is about 4.32. A fee that looks tiny each year compounds into a big gap.

cards.prompt: What is a share of ownership in a company called?
cards.example: A stock makes you a part owner, so you share in the company's gains and losses.
cards.note: Stock prices can swing a lot, but over long periods stocks have historically earned more than bonds. That higher expected return is payment for the higher risk.

cards.prompt: What do you hold when you lend money to a government or company in return for regular interest?
cards.example: A bond pays a fixed interest amount and returns the loan at the end of its term.
cards.note: As a bondholder you are a lender, not an owner. Bonds are usually calmer than stocks, but they still carry risks such as the borrower defaulting or rising interest rates.

cards.prompt: What is a share of company profit paid out to shareholders called?
cards.example: Dividend day came, and the company paid 1 per share after a profitable year.
cards.note: Dividends are optional: a company can raise, cut or skip them. When a dividend is paid, the share price typically drops by about that amount.

cards.prompt: Generally, a higher expected return comes with what?
cards.example: Higher risk is the price stocks charge for their higher expected returns compared with savings accounts.
cards.note: Investors demand extra reward for accepting uncertainty. If someone offers high returns with low risk, be very suspicious.

cards.prompt: What is it called when a price swings strongly up and down?
cards.example: Volatility was high that year, with the index moving several percent in a single week.
cards.note: High volatility means a wide range of possible outcomes in the short term. Money needed soon is usually kept away from very volatile assets.

cards.prompt: What describes how quickly an asset can be turned into cash without a big loss?
cards.example: Liquidity is high for a savings account, while a house can take months to sell.
cards.note: An emergency fund needs high liquidity. Assets that are hard to sell often have to be sold at a discount when you need cash fast.

cards.prompt: Which figure includes fees and shows the true yearly cost of a loan?
cards.example: Two loans with the same interest rate can have a different APR once fees are included.
cards.note: The plain interest rate ignores fees such as processing charges. To compare loans fairly, compare the APR or effective rate.

cards.prompt: What usually happens if you pay only the minimum on a credit card each month?
cards.example: High interest on the rest of the balance keeps piling up if you pay only the minimum.
cards.note: Credit card rates are often far higher than other loans, so the debt can grow faster than you repay it. Paying off a debt that costs 20% a year is like earning a guaranteed 20%.

cards.prompt: What is a plan for how you will spend and save your income called?
cards.example: Budget in hand, she saw that small daily purchases added up to a large monthly sum.
cards.note: A budget gives every unit of income a job before the month begins. Tracking actual spending for a few weeks is often the most eye-opening first step.

cards.prompt: In the 50/30/20 rule, what share of after-tax income goes to saving and paying off debt?
cards.example: Under the 50/30/20 rule, 20% is set aside for savings and extra debt payments.
cards.note: 50% goes to needs, 30% to wants and 20% to savings and debt. It is a simple starting point, not a law, and many people adjust the split.

cards.prompt: What is your income after taxes and other deductions called?
cards.example: Net income is the amount that actually lands in your bank account.
cards.note: Gross is the full amount before deductions, net is what remains. Budgets are best built on net income, because that is what you can actually spend.

cards.prompt: What is it called to invest a fixed amount at regular intervals, buying more units when prices are low?
cards.example: Dollar-cost averaging means the same monthly amount buys more shares in a dip and fewer at a peak.
cards.note: It spreads the entry price over time and removes the pressure to pick the perfect moment. It does not guarantee a profit, but it builds a steady habit.

cards.prompt: Complete the saying: '___ beats timing the market.'
cards.example: Time in the market beats timing the market, because nobody reliably predicts the next move.
cards.note: Many of the best days on the stock market come right after the worst ones. Investors who jump out often miss those rebounds.

cards.prompt: Which promise is a classic warning sign of investment fraud?
cards.example: Guaranteed high returns were the headline of the ad, exactly the red flag regulators warn about.
cards.note: High return always comes with risk, so nobody can honestly guarantee both. Pressure to decide quickly and secrecy are further warning signs.
